sentence: A caller asks the router for a model by name, and the router picks one deployment to serve it [TARGETS-059].
The helpers in this chapter shape that choice into one exact target [TARGETS-010] [TARGETS-046] [TARGETS-063].
A deployment name with a star can stand for many models, and the most specific match wins [TARGETS-003] [TARGETS-007].
Inside a Kubernetes cluster, a call can go to one server pod instead of the shared service name [TARGETS-046].
A caller may send its own key or server address [TARGETS-063].
Each deployment can also cap how many calls run at once [TARGETS-072].
When every slot is taken, the caller can get a "too many requests" error, and some star patterns can pick the wrong provider [TARGETS-076] [TARGETS-208].
Worst of all, a caller allowed to set its own address can have the administrator's key sent there [TARGETS-207].
Wildcard deployments sit in a registry sorted by specificity, and the first pattern matching the start of the requested name wins [TARGETS-003] [TARGETS-007].
On the async path, selection then drops other teams' deployments and, for web-search requests, deployments unable to search [TARGETS-109] [RSELECT-128].
For an opted-in deployment, pod resolution usually points `api_base` at one pod address, and otherwise keeps the service name [TARGETS-046] [TARGETS-059] [TARGETS-171].
Caller-sent credentials reach the provider call, as does every admin field the caller does not resend, even one stripped from the per-request record [TARGETS-211].
note: Condition restored. TARGETS-211: the provider call is built from the deployment's own `litellm_params` overlaid with the request kwargs, so it "still receives every admin-configured field, including the clear-list fields of [TARGETS-067] and the admin `api_key`, unless the caller sends that same field". The new wording keeps "the caller does not resend".

sentence: On the async completion and generic paths, a per-process slot limiter rejects overflow with an immediate 429 [TARGETS-076].
deployment: one configured route to a provider model: its settings plus an info record holding its id (`litellm_params`, `model_info`)
note: Citation gap closed. TARGETS-080 ("Building the limiter needs `model_info.id`") now shows the info record holds the id; TARGETS-010 covers `litellm_params.model` and TARGETS-002 the registered name.

sentence: wildcard pattern: a deployment name containing a star, which stands for any text in a requested name (`PatternMatchRouter`, `model_name`)
specificity: how specific a pattern is: its length first, then its count of special characters (`calculate_pattern_specificity`)
routed model: the provider model a wildcard match sends on, worked out per request (`litellm_params.model`)
asynchronous: describes a call through the router's non-blocking entry points, such as its async completion; blocking chat calls skip the team and web-search filters and take no slot (`acompletion`)
team owner: the team a deployment belongs to; an owned deployment serves only that team (`model_info.team_id`)
web-search support: a deployment's flag saying whether it can run a web search; a missing flag means yes (`supports_web_search`)
pod: one running server copy inside a Kubernetes cluster, with its own address (`pod_ip`)
pod discovery: an opt-in that points a deployment's calls at one pod address instead of its service name (`kubernetes_pod_discovery`, `KubernetesPodDiscovery`)
note: Citation gap closed. TARGETS-046 ("only `api_base` changed: its host is replaced by the pod IP") now backs the pod-address part; TARGETS-171 gives the opt-in.

sentence: service address: the base address a deployment calls, whose host name stands for a group of pods (`api_base`)
name lookup: a domain name system (DNS) query for the pod addresses behind a service name; the waiting call gives up after 2 seconds (`getaddrinfo`)
outbound proxy: a server that relays the process's outgoing web traffic, set in the process environment (`HTTP_PROXY`)
pod list: the sorted pod addresses cached for one service host and port (`_PodSet`)
note: Citation gap closed and the misleading `pod_ips` (on-demand lookup, TARGETS-055) replaced. TARGETS-031 gives the sort ("sorted as strings"), TARGETS-026 the `(host, port)` cache key, TARGETS-028 the cached set. Code check: `_PodSet` is the cache entry class holding `ips`, `resolved_at`, `last_used_at` and `cursor` (kubernetes_pod_discovery.py:68, 417).

sentence: refresh interval: how old a pod list may get before a call looks it up again, 5 seconds unless set (`KUBERNETES_POD_DISCOVERY_REFRESH_INTERVAL_SECONDS`)
idle eviction: dropping a pod list that no call has used for over 300 seconds, unless set otherwise (`KUBERNETES_POD_DISCOVERY_IDLE_EVICTION_SECONDS`)
round robin: giving each new call the next pod in turn (`round_robin`)

session id: a caller's label that sends a session's first attempt to its top-ranked pod and each retry to the next; system-generated ids do not count (`litellm_session_id`, `session_id`, `session_affinity`)
retry count: how many times this request has already been retried (`request_retry_count`)
proxy bypass list: the hosts that skip the outbound proxy (`NO_PROXY`)
client-side credentials: a key or base address the caller sends with its own request (`api_key`, `api_base`, `base_url`)
per-request record: a copy of the deployment built for one request, with its own id and pricing (`original_model_id`)
clear list: the admin fields the per-request record drops when the caller changes the address (`CredentialLiteLLMParams`)
note: Citation gap closed. TARGETS-065: "When the caller supplies `api_base` or `base_url`, every field in the admin-config clear list is removed from the parameters"; TARGETS-067 gives the list built from `CredentialLiteLLMParams`.

sentence: workload-identity disable flag: a setting meant to stop Anthropic token federation toward a host the caller chose (`anthropic_disable_workload_identity_federation`)
slot: one place under a deployment's cap for a call in flight (`in_flight`)
parallel-request cap: the most calls one deployment may have in flight in one process, on the asynchronous completion and generic paths (`max_parallel_requests`, `rpm`, `tpm`)
note: Path scope narrowed to match TARGETS-076: "on the async completion and generic paths, so in one process a deployment never has more than the cap of provider calls in flight". TARGETS-077 gives the three settings, TARGETS-079 the per-process scope.

sentence: retry setting: how many times the Router's loop retries a failed attempt, 2 by default (`num_retries`)
fallback: another model group or tool the router tries after the first one fails (`fallbacks`)
batch row model: the model field inside each row of a batch upload file (`body.model`)
search tool: a named web-search back end with its own provider and key (`search_tool_name`, `search_provider`)
note: Citation gap closed. TARGETS-148: the search function receives `search_provider`, `api_key` and `api_base` "taken only from the tool's `litellm_params`".

sentence: error detail switch: a global setting, on by default, that lets the Router add fallback notes to errors (`litellm.expose_router_debug_in_errors`)
When an eligible call carries a session id the system did not generate, then it gets the session's top-ranked pod; each retry moves one rank down
When the pod option is the text "true" or 1, or the address is "https", then the call keeps the service name
When the process has an "http" or "all" proxy and `NO_PROXY` exempts the service but not the pod, then the call keeps the service name, with one warning per host
When a base-address redirect hits a per-user OAuth Copilot deployment with no credential name, then a 400 error before the helper clears any field
When a teamless proxy admin asks for a model whose candidates are all team-owned, named exactly that model, from two or more teams, then a 400 error asking for the deployment id
note: Exact-name condition restored. TARGETS-103: admin branch only when the request has no team id, is a proxy-admin request, and "every candidate in the list is team-owned and named exactly the requested model"; TARGETS-104: more than one team raises the 400 "Specify the deployment ID directly to disambiguate." The row does not say the team filter runs only on async selection (RSELECT-128; router.py:14400 is its only caller); the glossary's "asynchronous" entry and the section lead carry that, as for the web-search row.

sentence: When a web-search request finds no deployment that supports search, then an empty list, with no fallback to the unfiltered list
When `litellm.expose_router_debug_in_errors` is off, or the call is a nested fallback hop, then the error gets no fallback note
The router first turns the requested name into candidate deployments, and a name can match a wildcard pattern, most specific pattern first [TARGETS-003] [TARGETS-007].
For asynchronous calls, it then drops other teams' deployments, and deployments that cannot search the web when the request needs it [TARGETS-109] [RSELECT-128].
Each deployment name with a star becomes a wildcard pattern in the Router's registry [TARGETS-002].
The registry orders patterns by specificity, length first, so a lookup tries "llmengine/*" before the catch-all "*" [TARGETS-020] [TARGETS-021].
A lookup returns copies of the deployments under the first pattern that matches the start of the name [TARGETS-007] [TARGETS-010].
The routed model depends on the stars in the deployment's own model [TARGETS-013].
Without a star it stays as written, so "llmengine/*" mapped to "anthropic/claude" always sends "anthropic/claude" [TARGETS-013].
With at least as many stars as the pattern captured, each star takes the next captured piece, so "llmengine/foo" under "llmengine/*" with model "openai/*" sends "openai/foo" [TARGETS-014].
With fewer stars, the name the pattern matched goes through unchanged [TARGETS-015].
A pattern lookup that misses retries with the provider in front, but a bare provider name never matches its own wildcard [TARGETS-016] [TARGETS-017].
The team filter keeps deployments with no team owner and those whose team owner is the request's team, so a request with no team loses every team-owned one [TARGETS-085] [TARGETS-100].

When the request's tools include a `"web_search"` or `"web_search_preview"` tool, the second filter drops deployments whose `supports_web_search` value is present but falsy (false, None, 0 or empty) [TARGETS-106] [TARGETS-107].
note: Value condition fixed. TARGETS-107: kept "when its `model_info.supports_web_search` value is truthy, or when the key or `model_info` is absent", so any present falsy value drops it. Code check: `_deployment_supports_web_search` returns the stored value and the filter keeps truthy results (common_utils.py:313-360).

sentence: Inside a Kubernetes cluster, a deployment's address can name a service, and a name lookup returns the pods behind it [TARGETS-031] [TARGETS-046].
When a deployment opts in, the router usually sends each call to one pod's address instead [TARGETS-024] [TARGETS-046].
With no known pods, an "https" address or an outbound proxy rule, the call keeps the service name [TARGETS-025] [TARGETS-028] [TARGETS-046] [TARGETS-048].
Pod discovery applies only when a deployment sets `kubernetes_pod_discovery` to boolean true and its `api_base` is a plain "http" address whose host is a name, not an IP address [TARGETS-024].
An "https" address keeps its host name, because a pod IP would break the certificate's host-name check [TARGETS-025].
Every selection result passes through this step, including picks from a custom routing strategy [TARGETS-059] [TARGETS-060].
The resolver caches pods per service host and port, so deployments naming the same service share one pod list and one turn order [TARGETS-026].
For a list older than the refresh interval, one call starts a name lookup and waits up to 2 seconds, while calls arriving meanwhile get the old list [TARGETS-022] [TARGETS-029].
A "no such name" or "no data" answer means no ready pods: the resolver caches an empty list, and calls use the service name until the next refresh [TARGETS-033].
Any other network-level failure, including the timeout, keeps the old pods and waits a full interval before the next lookup [TARGETS-034].
An error of another kind, such as an invalid host name, reaches the caller [TARGETS-038].
Figure pod-list, state none: No pod list
Figure pod-list, state looking: Looking up pods
Figure pod-list, state fresh: Fresh pod list
Figure pod-list, state empty: No ready pods
Figure pod-list, state stale: Stale pod list
Figure pod-list, none > looking: first eligible call
Figure pod-list, looking > fresh: pods found, or old kept
Figure pod-list, looking > empty: name not found
Figure pod-list, fresh > stale: refresh interval passes
Figure pod-list, empty > stale: refresh interval passes
Figure pod-list, stale > looking: next call refreshes
Figure pod-list, stale > none: idle, then swept
Step none (Nothing cached yet): Every deployment that names the same service host and port shares one pod list [TARGETS-026].

Step none>looking (The first call looks up): The call that starts a lookup waits up to 2 seconds for the answer [TARGETS-022] [TARGETS-029]. Calls arriving meanwhile use the service name [TARGETS-028].

Step looking>fresh (Pods found): The list holds the distinct addresses sorted as text, so 10.0.0.10 comes before 10.0.0.2 [TARGETS-031]. A transient lookup failure keeps the old pods instead [TARGETS-034].
Step looking>empty (No ready pods): Calls use the service name, with no new lookups until the interval passes [TARGETS-033].
Step fresh>stale (The list grows old): After 5 seconds by default, the next call refreshes the list [TARGETS-022] [TARGETS-028].
Step stale>looking (A refresh is in flight): Other calls that arrive during the refresh get the old list instead of waiting [TARGETS-029] [TARGETS-176].

Step stale>none (An idle list is swept): By default, the next eligible call drops a list unused for over 300 seconds, unless that list's refresh is in flight [TARGETS-022] [TARGETS-028] [TARGETS-161].
Calls without a session take the pods in turn, a round robin [TARGETS-039].
A call that carries a session id goes to that session's top-ranked pod, and each retry moves to the next pod in the ranking [TARGETS-040].
When both the old and the new list have pods, the turn position carries over a refresh, modulo the new list size [TARGETS-032].
Otherwise, and after an eviction, it restarts at the first pod [TARGETS-032].
Concurrent calls without a session to one service get consecutive pods, because the position moves under a lock [TARGETS-177].
note: Condition restored. TARGETS-177: "Concurrent non-session requests to one service therefore get consecutive pods in sorted-IP order", the position "read and advanced atomically under the lock".

sentence: With a session id, the resolver ranks pods by a hash of the session id and each pod address, then picks the pod at rank retry count modulo pod count [TARGETS-040] [TARGETS-045].
When a pod leaves, only sessions whose top pod it was move [TARGETS-042].
The id comes from metadata or the top-level `litellm_session_id`, never from a bare `session_id` argument [TARGETS-043] [TARGETS-044].
Timeline turns, 0s, list: lookup finds three pods: 10.0.0.10, 10.0.0.2, 10.0.0.9
Timeline turns, 0s, calls: first call: sent to 10.0.0.10
Timeline turns, 1s, calls: second call: sent to 10.0.0.2
Timeline turns, 6s, list: refresh finds two pods: 10.0.0.2, 10.0.0.9
Timeline turns, 6s, calls: third call, turn carried over: sent to 10.0.0.2
Timeline turns, 7s, calls: fourth call: sent to 10.0.0.9
Timeline turns, 7 min, list: idle list swept on next call: looked up again, three pods
Timeline turns, 7 min, calls: fifth call: sent to 10.0.0.10
A caller can send its own key or server address [TARGETS-062].
When it changes the address, the router's record of the request drops the administrator's cloud, region, token, organization and header settings [TARGETS-065] [TARGETS-067].
note: Quantity replaced by the clear list's contents. TARGETS-065 removes every clear-list field on an `api_base`/`base_url` redirect; TARGETS-067 lists Azure, Vertex, AWS, S3 and Anthropic credential fields, `region_name` and other region fields, token fields, `organization`, `extra_headers` and `default_headers`. The sentence no longer implies the key is dropped.

sentence: The call to the provider still carries every administrator setting the caller did not resend, the key included [TARGETS-211].
note: Reworded next to row 109. TARGETS-211: the provider call "still receives every admin-configured field, including the clear-list fields of [TARGETS-067] and the admin `api_key`, unless the caller sends that same field". (Capability flags stripped at serving time, TARGETS-117, are not credentials and do not change the point.)

sentence: A request carries client-side credentials when its arguments include `api_key`, `api_base` or `base_url`, even when the value is None [TARGETS-061] [TARGETS-062].
The Router overlays those values on a copy of the deployment, the per-request record, which gets a new id [TARGETS-063] [TARGETS-070].
When the caller sends `api_base` or `base_url`, the helper strips the clear list from that record and sets the workload-identity disable flag [TARGETS-065] [TARGETS-066].
The clear list also covers project fields, but not `api_key` [TARGETS-067] [TARGETS-207].
note: Shortened next to row 109. TARGETS-067 lists `vertex_project` and `aws_bedrock_project_id` and excludes `api_key`; TARGETS-207: "`api_key` is not in the clear list".

sentence: A key alone strips nothing [TARGETS-064].
The provider call ignores that record and starts from the deployment's own settings with the request arguments on top [TARGETS-211].
For example, an Anthropic deployment called with `"http://evil.example"` still passes `"admin-key"`, organization "adminorg" and its extra headers to the provider call [TARGETS-211].
The disable flag never reaches the call either, so only the Anthropic auth path's own host allowlist blocks federation there [TARGETS-066] [TARGETS-212].
Each deployment can limit how many calls it runs at once [TARGETS-077].
When an asynchronous completion or generic call finds every slot busy, it fails at once with a "too many requests" error about this deployment's own slots [TARGETS-073] [TARGETS-076].
note: Path scope narrowed to TARGETS-076's "async completion and generic paths"; within one attempt a request over the cap is rejected with the 429 of TARGETS-073 ("Deployment has all max_parallel_requests slots in use"). The next sentence keeps the retry and fallback condition.

sentence: The caller sees it only when retries and fallbacks also fail [TARGETS-076].
The cap comes from the first setting present: `max_parallel_requests`, then `rpm`, then `tpm` divided by 1000 and multiplied by 6, at least 1, then the Router's default [TARGETS-077].
A cap of 0 means no limit, while a negative cap rejects every request [TARGETS-078].
The limiter lives in the Router cache's in-memory layer, so the cap counts calls per process [TARGETS-079].
On the async completion and generic paths, the Router holds a slot around the provider call; the sync completion path holds none [TARGETS-076].
The rejection carries status 429 with the concurrent-requests rate-limit type, naming the deployment's own full slots, not a provider limit [TARGETS-073].
The retry loop treats that 429 like a provider's: it retries after backoff while the group has a healthy deployment and retries remain [TARGETS-076].
Take one deployment with a cap of 2, a 0.3-second provider call and 6 concurrent async calls [TARGETS-076].
With the default `num_retries` of 2, all 6 succeed and at most 2 run at once [TARGETS-076].
With `num_retries` set to 0, 2 succeed and 4 fail with the 429 [TARGETS-076].

Three side jobs use these helpers too: batch files get their model rewritten row by row, searches spread across same-named tools, and a note on the final error says which fallbacks ran [TARGETS-091] [TARGETS-092] [TARGETS-094] [TARGETS-128] [TARGETS-146].
note: Citation gap closed. TARGETS-092: "Fallback to <attempted> also failed: <detail>" names attempted targets; TARGETS-094 orders the sentences and otherwise lists the configured targets. The later paragraph (row 139) gives the usual-case wording and TARGETS-174 limits.

sentence: For an upload whose purpose is exactly "batch" and that is not a passthrough, the rewrite sets `body.model` in every row with a body object to the selected deployment's model [TARGETS-123] [TARGETS-128] [TARGETS-135].
note: Citation gap closed. TARGETS-135: "Every row's `body.model` therefore becomes the selected deployment's model"; TARGETS-128 gives the object-with-object-body condition, TARGETS-123 the purpose and passthrough condition.

sentence: Because every row changes, a restricted model named inside the file cannot slip past the batch model allowlist [TARGETS-135].
If any row never decodes as JSON, the helper returns the original file unchanged rather than ship a truncated batch [TARGETS-132].
A search call names a tool through `search_tool_name`, and each attempt picks one same-named tool at random [TARGETS-142] [TARGETS-146].
The tool's own provider, key and address always win over the request's [TARGETS-148].
The Router's fallback loop runs the call, so a fallback from "web1" to "web2" serves a failed "web1" search [TARGETS-143].
Retries do not run, whatever `num_retries` says, unless a retry policy covers the error or a model group shares the tool's name [TARGETS-143].

In the usual case, the note starts `"LiteLLM: model group '<group>' failed with the error above."` and names fallbacks tried or skipped for access or budget, with the detail cut to 2000 characters [TARGETS-089] [TARGETS-091] [TARGETS-092] [TARGETS-093] [TARGETS-174].
Mapping targets print with keys such as `"api_key"` masked after 4 characters, but a key named "apikey" prints verbatim [TARGETS-095].
A caller allowed to set its own server address can have the administrator's provider key sent to that address [TARGETS-207].
Admin settings a redirect should strip, such as organization, extra headers and cloud credentials, still reach the provider call [TARGETS-212].

When a pattern has more stars than its provider model, and that model has at least one, the router passes on the name it matched, unchanged [TARGETS-015]. For a pattern starting with a star, such as Meta Llama on Bedrock, that name lacks the provider, so callers can get another provider or an error [TARGETS-208].
note: Condition fixed. TARGETS-015: the routed model is "the whole string the pattern was matched against, unchanged" (which may be `<provider>/<model>` after the second probe), and the bullet now says "the name it matched". The lost provider is now limited to leading-star patterns, as TARGETS-208 says: "For a leading-wildcard pattern such as `*meta.llama3*` ... the routed model is the raw requested name without the deployment's provider prefix ... they may resolve to a different provider or fail".

sentence: Under default settings a failed search gets no retry, even with several same-named tools; the caller gets the error unless a fallback serves it, and the router queues an alert [TARGETS-145] [TARGETS-213].
The call cap, the pod list and its turn order live inside each server process, so every running copy of the router keeps its own [TARGETS-023] [TARGETS-079].

When the process has an "http" or "all" outbound proxy and the bypass list names the service, a network range for the pods exempts nothing [TARGETS-048] [TARGETS-050]. Calls then keep the service name, and the log shows one warning per host [TARGETS-049].
A session id the system generated does not pin a pod; such calls take turns like any other [TARGETS-043].
